title: Sharing an Email Quota
statement: An email provider accepts 1,000 emails per second, counting retries. Transactional emails such as receipts peak at 150 per second and must arrive within 1 minute. A campaign of 5 million emails must finish within 3 hours. Exercise assumptions: the pacer can keep separate queues and always take one first; the team prefers the campaign to finish as early as possible.
constraints: Never more than 1,000 per second; prefer the campaign to finish early.

approaches.name: Two queues; transactional always first; the campaign uses whatever room is left, at least 850 per second
approaches.hint: Urgent first, campaign fills the rest
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: Campaign at least 850 per second: under 1.7 hours
approaches.why: Transactional email never waits behind the campaign, so it arrives within the minute; the campaign always has at least 1,000 − 150 = 850 per second, finishing within 5,000,000 ÷ 850 ≈ 5,900 seconds, about 1.6 hours, and the pacer never passes 1,000.

approaches.name: Two queues with a fixed split: 400 per second for transactional, 600 for the campaign
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Transactional email has more room than its 150 peak and the campaign finishes in 5,000,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 2.3 hours, within 3, but unused transactional room is wasted, so the campaign ends later than it could, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: One queue in arrival order
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: A receipt behind the campaign waits up to about 1.4 hours
approaches.why: Once the campaign is queued, a receipt waits behind up to 5 million emails at 1,000 per second, about 1.4 hours, far beyond 1 minute.

title: A Crash Around a Send
statement: Workers send promotional emails. A worker can crash at any moment, and its message is then delivered to another worker. The email provider accepts an idempotency key and drops a repeated request with the same key. Exercise assumptions: a user must never get the same promotion twice; the team prefers that no promotion is missed either.
constraints: A crash can happen between any two steps.

approaches.name: Record the key as "sending", send with the key as the provider's idempotency key, then record "sent"; a redelivered message in "sending" is sent again with the same key
approaches.hint: Let the provider drop the repeat
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: One send, or a retry the provider drops
approaches.why: A crash before sending leads to a send on redelivery; a crash after sending leads to a retry with the same key, which the provider drops. No duplicate and no miss.

approaches.name: Record the key as "sent", then send without the provider's key; a redelivered message that finds the key is skipped
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: A promotion is never sent twice, but a crash after recording and before sending means the user never gets it, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: Send without the provider's key, then record "sent"
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: A crash after sending and before recording makes the next worker send again, so the user gets the promotion twice.

title: Preferences During Retries
statement: A promotional push to a user fails and is retried with backoff for up to 2 hours. Exercise assumptions: if the user opts out of promotions, no attempt may start more than 5 minutes after the opt-out; reading preferences costs one database lookup per attempt, which the database can afford; the team prefers an opt-out to take effect as soon as possible.
examples: Attempts at 0, 1, 5, 20 and 60 minutes after the first failure.
constraints: No attempt more than 5 minutes after an opt-out.
One lookup per attempt is affordable.
Prefer the opt-out to apply at once.

approaches.name: Read the preferences from the database just before every attempt
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Every attempt sees the latest choice, so an opt-out applies to the very next attempt.

approaches.name: Read the preferences before every attempt from a cache that can be up to 1 minute old
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: An opt-out reaches the check within 1 minute, inside the 5-minute rule, but attempts in that minute still go out, against the preference for an immediate effect.

approaches.name: Read the preferences once, before the first attempt
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: A user who opts out after the first attempt still gets retries for up to 2 hours, breaking the 5-minute rule.
